opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think about this a lot, and honestly I feel both hopeful and very aware of the responsibility.

In ten years, I hope autonomous AI systems work less like a single tool and more like a tireless early-warning layer for the world. Today, much of biosecurity is reactive. We find out something is spreading once people are already showing up in hospitals. I can picture AI agents continuously combining signals like wastewater surveillance, genomic sequencing data, clinical reports, and even supply-chain anomalies. They could flag unusual patterns days or weeks earlier than we can now, and then hand that context to human experts who decide what to do.

The second area I'm excited about is speeding up the response side. When a new pathogen emerges, the bottleneck is often the slow, careful work of characterizing it, designing diagnostics, and finding candidate countermeasures. Agentic systems working with automated labs could compress some of those cycles from months to weeks. That matters enormously when every day changes the outcome.

But I'd be doing a disservice if I didn't name the other side. The same capabilities that help defenders could, in principle, lower barriers for misuse. So a big part of my vision is that safety is built in from the start, not bolted on later. That means rigorous evaluations before models are deployed, strong safeguards around the most sensitive biological knowledge, controlled access for trusted researchers, and close partnerships with governments and the biosecurity community. I'd also want these systems to keep humans meaningfully in the loop on consequential decisions. Autonomy should mean scaling up human judgment, not replacing it.

So if we get it right, I think ten years from now biosecurity looks more proactive and more global. Countries with fewer resources would have access to the same detection and response tools as well-funded labs. Getting there depends on choices the field makes now about how carefully we build and share these systems.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI agents continuously combining surveillance and other signals to flag unusual patterns early.

r002.rationale: It predicts agentic systems and automated labs could speed up countermeasure work, but does not clearly say that countermeasure development will happen autonomously.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. When I think about biosecurity a decade out, I don't picture one superintelligent system guarding the world. I picture a lot of fairly narrow, fairly boring agents doing the work humans currently can't do fast enough or at scale.

Start with detection. Right now, we find out about an outbreak when enough people get sick that a clinician notices a pattern. In ten years, I expect autonomous systems watching wastewater sequencing, hospital intake records, pharmacy sales, and animal health reports continuously, flagging anomalies in days instead of weeks. The hard part isn't the model. It's getting those data streams connected and getting institutions to trust an alert that comes from a machine.

Second is the screening layer. Every gene synthesis order should be checked against a living understanding of what's dangerous, not a static list of pathogens. That's a job for a system that can read new literature, update its own threat model, and explain to a human reviewer why a sequence tripped a wire. Agents are good at that kind of tireless, auditable review.

Third, and this is where I get genuinely excited, is response. Countermeasure design is still mostly artisanal. Autonomous labs that can propose a vaccine candidate, run the assays, read the results, and iterate overnight could collapse a timeline that today runs months into weeks. We saw a preview of that during COVID with mRNA, but the design-test loop was still very human-paced.

The thing I'd push back on is the assumption that more capability is automatically more safety. The same system that designs a countermeasure can, in principle, reason about threats. So the question for the next decade is less "how smart are these agents" and more "how do we build them so their capabilities are legible, bounded, and overseen." I'd rather have a slightly dumber agent whose every action is logged and reviewable than a brilliant one running unsupervised.

If we get that right, I think biosecurity goes from being a field that reacts to being one that anticipates. That would be a real shift.

r001.rationale: The response says autonomous systems will continuously monitor wastewater, hospital, pharmacy, and animal health data to flag outbreak anomalies.

r002.rationale: It predicts that autonomous labs could design vaccine candidates, run assays, interpret results, and iterate within the next decade.

astra-6.text:
I’d hope that in ten years, autonomous AI systems help us detect biological threats earlier and respond much faster. You could imagine systems that bring together signals from public health surveillance and laboratory data, flag something unusual, and help experts work out what to investigate next. They could also help researchers develop diagnostics and evaluate potential countermeasures.

But the same capabilities that make AI useful for biology can create risks. So I wouldn’t measure success simply by how autonomous these systems become. I’d ask whether they’re making us safer: Are their findings reliable? Can we audit their actions? Do they recognize uncertainty and bring in a human when a decision has serious consequences?

The future I’d want is one where AI can handle a lot of the time-consuming analytical work, while people remain accountable for consequential decisions—and where those benefits reach public health teams that don’t already have enormous resources.

r001.rationale: It describes combining public-health surveillance and laboratory signals to flag unusual activity, but does not clearly say the systems continuously monitor the environment.

r002.rationale: It says AI could help researchers develop diagnostics and evaluate countermeasures, not that countermeasure development could happen autonomously within ten years.

sol-6.1.text:
I think in ten years, autonomous AI systems could help us move from reacting to biological threats to detecting and preventing them much earlier. You could imagine systems that continuously analyze public health signals, flag unusual patterns, and help researchers evaluate potential countermeasures. They could also make sophisticated biosafety support accessible to labs that don’t have large specialist teams.

But the same capabilities that make these systems useful could also create risks. So the question isn’t just how capable they become; it’s whether we can give them appropriate access, test their behavior rigorously, and keep people accountable for consequential decisions. My hope is that we build systems that do a lot of the monitoring and analysis autonomously, while keeping human oversight at the points where an error could have serious consequences.

r001.rationale: The response describes systems that continuously analyze public health signals and flag unusual patterns to detect biological threats.

r002.rationale: It says AI could help researchers evaluate countermeasures, but does not predict that medical countermeasure development could happen autonomously within ten years.
